segments.translit: jagadarthakaruṇābhārastimitahṛdayāḥ kṛṣṇācāryapādās tam evārthaṃ viśeṣay[i]tu[m] āhuḥ—
segments.translation: [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}, his heart moist with the weight of [compassion]{karuna} for the good of the world, speaks to specify that same point further:
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.07.m1) introduces the song as spoken by [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}, his heart moist with [compassion]{karuna} for the world, to specify further ‘that same point’, which the segment does not name. The Tibetan translation instead has him speak ‘the exalted meaning of reality’.

flags.note: Where the Sanskrit has tam evārthaṃ viśeṣayitum āhuḥ, ‘speaks to specify that same point’, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de kho na nyid kyi don khyad par du 'phags pa gsungs te, ‘spoke the exalted (distinguished) meaning of reality’. It seems to have read tattva-, ‘reality’, for tam eva, and taken viśeṣayitum as an adjective. I translate the Sanskrit.

What ‘that same point’ (tam evārtham) refers back to is not stated in the segment; perhaps what the preceding songs taught. stimita can mean ‘moist’ or ‘motionless’; the Tibetan thugs brlan pa, ‘heart moistened’, supports ‘moist’.
The printed hadayāḥ is read hṛdayāḥ, ‘heart’ (Tibetan thugs). viśeṣa[i]yatu[m] contains Shastri’s restorations, read viśeṣayitum.

segments.translit: ālītyādi | uktārthasvadevatāyogapūrvakavajrajāpopadeśaṃ labdhvā kṛṣṇācāryeṇa ālinā lokajñānena kālinā lokabhāsena ca ekīkṛtya avadhūtīmārgaṃ sudṛḍhaṃ ruddhataṃ punaḥ sadguruprasādāt prakṛtipariśuddhāvadhūtikārūpeṇa kṛṣṇācāryapādā viśiṣṭamanaso bhūtāḥ |
segments.translation: ‘[Āli]{ali}…’ and so on. Having received the [instruction]{upadesa} in [vajra recitation]{vajrajapa}, preceded by his own [deity yoga]{devatayoga} as explained before, [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha}, unifying by means of [āli]{ali}, the knowledge that is [light]{aloka}, and [kāli]{kali}, the [spreading of light]{alokabhasa}, firmly blocked the path of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}. Then, by the grace of the [true guru]{guru}, [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} became of distinguished mind, in the form of the naturally purified [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}.
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.07.m2) reads [āli]{ali} and [kāli]{kali} as the light and the spreading of light: instructed in vajra recitation, Kṛṣṇācārya, unifying through them, firmly blocks the path of the [avadhūtī]{avadhuti}. Where the song has Kāṇha grow [downcast]{vimana}, his paraphrase has him become ‘of distinguished mind’. The Tibetan translation instead holds the unified pair still within that path.

equations.en: the knowledge that is light (lokajñāna, probably for ālokajñāna)
the spreading of light (lokabhāsa, probably for ālokābhāsa)

flags.note: Shastri prints ālinā lokajñānena kālinā lokabhāsena. The unbroken script probably had ālinālokajñānena, kālinālokābhāsena, where sandhi hides an initial ā. That gives ālokajñāna, ‘the knowledge that is light’, and ālokābhāsa, ‘spreading of light’, the Guhyasamāja terms, which the Tibetan ye shes kyi snang ba and snang ba mched pa support. I translate accordingly.
ruddhataṃ is not a clear form: perhaps ruddhaṃ followed by taṃ, or ruddham followed by tataḥ, ‘then’. I read ‘firmly blocked’ and take punaḥ with the next sentence, as the Tibetan does (slar yang).

ekīkṛtya, ‘unifying, making one’, has no expressed object, and avadhūtīmārgaṃ is accusative though kṛṣṇācāryeṇa … ruddham is passive. I take the path as what is blocked, echoing the song's ‘blocked the road’. The path could instead be the goal of the unifying (‘making them one in the avadhūtī's path’), with ruddham impersonal (‘held firmly’).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads 'jigs byed ni ye shes kyi snang ba dang dus mtshan ma ni snang ba mched pa gcig tu byas nas a wa d+hU tI'i lam du brtan pa dang 'gog pa'o. There light and spreading of light are made one and then ‘held firm and stopped in the path of the avadhūtī’: what is stopped is the unified pair, not the path. Its names for āli and kāli, 'jigs byed (‘the terrifying’) and dus mtshan ma (‘night’), are those of its version of the song.

segments.translit:
kāhnu kahim̐ gai ityādi | dhruvapadena nijavāsāropaṇakhaṇḍanam āhuḥ | svayam evātmānaṃ saṃbodhya vadanti | bhoḥ kṛṣṇavajrapādāḥ vyāpyavyāpakarūpeṇa sukhena vyāpitaṃ jagat iti | śrīmaddherukatantrarājoktārtham āmukhīkaraṇāt kutra sthāne asmābhir nivāsaḥ karaṇīyaḥ sa tanmayatvāt ye ’pi yogino manogocarā manendriyabodhapradhānā bhavanti te ’py asmin dharme udāsāḥ su(sa)dūratarā eva |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ—
jāhi maṇa pavaṇa na sañcarai
ravi śaśi nāhi paveśa |
tahi vaṭa cīa visāmakara
sarahem̐ kahi uvavesa ||
segments.translation: ‘[Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, where shall I go…’ and so on. With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he speaks of breaking down the imputing of a [dwelling]{nivasa} of one’s own. Addressing himself, he says: ‘O [Kṛṣṇavajrapāda]{p-kanha}, the world is pervaded by [bliss]{sukha}, in the form of [pervaded and pervader]{vyapya-vyapaka}.’ Because he has made directly present the meaning stated in the glorious [Heruka Tantra]{tx-heruka-tantra}, king of tantras, he asks: in what place am I to make my [dwelling]{nivasa}, since it is made of that? Even those [yogis]{yogi} who stay within the [range of the mind]{manogocara}, in whom understanding through the mind-sense predominates, they too stand [indifferent]{udasa} to this [dharma]{dharma}, very far removed indeed. As [Sarahapāda]{p-saraha} says: ‘Where mind and [wind]{vayu} do not move, / where [sun]{surya} and [moon]{moon} have no entry, / there, fool, let the [mind]{citta} rest: / [Saraha]{p-saraha} has given this [instruction]{upadesa}.’
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.07.m3) says the refrain undoes the imputing of a [dwelling]{nivasa} of one’s own: the world is pervaded by bliss, leaving nowhere to make one. Yogis within ‘the [range of the mind]{manogocara}’, understanding chiefly through the mind-sense, stand [indifferent]{udasa} to this dharma, far from it. The Tibetan translation makes his question a statement: one dwells by oneself.

citations.quoted: Where mind and wind do not move, where sun and moon have no entry, there, fool, let the mind rest: Saraha has given this instruction.
citations.work: Saraha (named by Munidatta); probably his Apabhraṃśa Dohākoṣa

citations.quoted: The world is pervaded by bliss, in the form of pervaded and pervader (apparently the meaning Munidatta says is stated in the Heruka Tantra; not given as a verbatim quotation).
citations.work: Heruka Tantra, so named by Munidatta; whether a Hevajra or a Cakrasaṃvara tantra is meant is uncertain

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has kye nag po spyod pa pa rdo rje'i tshig, ‘O Kṛṣṇacaryāpa, the vajra word:’. It apparently read -vajrapada as ‘vajra word’ where the Sanskrit has the name Kṛṣṇavajrapāda in the vocative. It also has bde ba chen pos, ‘by great bliss’, for sukhena, ‘by bliss’.

Where the Sanskrit asks kutra sthāne asmābhir nivāsaḥ karaṇīyaḥ, ‘in what place am I to make my dwelling?’, the Tibetan translation makes a statement: gang du gnas 'cha' ba ni bdag nyid kyis gnas par byed pa'o, ‘making a dwelling somewhere is dwelling by oneself’. It renders nijavāsāropaṇakhaṇḍana loosely as rang gis gnas su 'gog pas 'gog pa, with no word for ‘imputing’.

sa tanmayatvāt, ‘it, because of being made of that’: sa is masculine and cannot refer to jagat, ‘world’ (neuter). It may mean the dwelling, or the text may be damaged. The Tibetan thams cad de'i rang bzhin yin pa'i phyir, ‘because everything is of its nature’, suggests sarva-, ‘all’, and joins the phrase to the next sentence. I take ‘that’ as the bliss just named and keep the phrase with the question.

manendriya- stands for manaindriya-, ‘the mind-sense’ (Tibetan yid kyi dbang po). In Saraha's verse, vaṭa is taken as ‘fool’ (Sanskrit vaṭu, ‘lad’, used in contempt), with the Tibetan rmongs pa. The honorific plurals (vadanti, asmābhiḥ) are rendered as singular.

Munidatta applies the song’s uāsa (udāsa) to yogis who stand indifferent to this dharma. Since he adds sudūratara, ‘very far removed’, he means estrangement, not the praiseworthy detachment the word can also denote. Shastri prints su(sa)dūratarā.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena taṃ dyotayanta āhuḥ—
te tini ityādi | bāhye svargamartyarasātalam adhyātme kāyavākcittadivārātrisandhyāyogayoginītantrādikaṃ boddhavyaṃ | etair anyonyaṃ mahāsukhavyāpakatvena bhedopalabdhilakṣaṇaṃ nāsti yogināṃ paramārthavidām |
tathā cāgamaḥ—
svargamartyapātālam ekamūrti bhavet kṣaṇāt | iti vacanāt etadarthaṃ caryāpādenoktam asti |
ātem̐ tisem̐ nava tisim̐ em̐ tia maṇḍala nāhi viseṣe ityādi vistaraṃ sakaladharmādhigamanena kṛṣṇācāryapādā vadanti | bhavavikalpacchedakā vayam iti |
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada}, illuminating that, he says: ‘Those three…’ and so on. Outwardly, heaven, earth and the underworld; inwardly, body, speech and [mind]{citta}; day, night and twilight; the yoga and yoginī tantras and the rest: these are to be understood. For [yogis]{yogi} who know the [ultimate]{paramartha}, since [great bliss]{mahasukha} pervades them, there is no mark of perceiving difference among these, one from another. So the scripture says: ‘Heaven, earth and the underworld would become of one form in an instant.’ On the strength of this statement, this meaning is expressed in a verse of a song of [conduct]{carya}: ‘Thirty-seven, nine, thirty-eight: among these three [maṇḍalas]{mandala} there is no distinction’, and so on, at length. Having understood all [dharmas]{dharma}, [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} says: ‘I cut off the [concepts]{vikalpa} of [existence]{bhava}.’
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.07.m4) takes ‘those three’ as triads: heaven, earth and underworld; body, speech and mind; day, night and twilight. Since [great bliss]{mahasukha} pervades them, yogis who know the ultimate perceive no difference among them; he does not explain ‘split apart’. ‘[Existence]{bhava} is cut off’ becomes Kṛṣṇācārya saying he cuts off the concepts of existence.

equations.en: the triads: outwardly heaven, earth and the underworld; inwardly body, speech and mind; day, night and twilight; the yoga and yoginī tantras and the rest

citations.quoted: Heaven, earth and the underworld would become of one form in an instant.
Thirty-seven, nine, thirty-eight: among these three maṇḍalas there is no distinction (and so on, at length).
citations.work: unidentified caryā song (caryāpāda); the Tibetan translation treats caryāpāda as the name of its author

flags.note: The Apabhraṃśa verse ātem̐ tisem̐ nava tisim̐ em̐ tia maṇḍala nāhi viseṣe is garbled; only ‘these three maṇḍalas … no distinction’ (em̐ tia maṇḍala nāhi viseṣe) is clear. For the numbers I follow the Tibetan translation, sum cu bdun dang dgu dang sum cu brgyad / de rnams dkyil 'khor gsum la khyad par med, ‘thirty-seven and nine and thirty-eight: in these three maṇḍalas there is no distinction’. The Bengali may hide Prakrit sattatīsa (37) or aṭṭhatīsa (38). A guess, unverified: the numbers count the deities of three maṇḍalas (the Vajradhātu maṇḍala of the yoga tantras has thirty-seven, the Hevajra maṇḍala nine), which would fit the compound's mention of yoga and yoginī tantras.

The compound kāyavākcittadivārātrisandhyāyogayoginītantrādikaṃ can list ‘the yoga and yoginī tantras and the rest’ among the things to be understood as the three, as translated, or name where the triads are taught. The Tibetan takes it the second way: day, night and twilight are to be understood rnal 'byor ma'i rgyud la sogs par, ‘in the yoginī tantras and so on’, with no word for ‘yoga’.

The song says the three are bhinna (‘split apart’ or ‘different’), and the Tibetan translation of the song has so sor 'dug, ‘remain separate’. Munidatta instead says that yogis who know the ultimate perceive no difference among the triads. He does not gloss bhinna (perhaps he took it as ‘broken’, the distinctions dissolved). I have not harmonized them.

caryāpādena, ‘by a verse (pāda) of a caryā song’, is instrumental singular, while Munidatta names authors in the honorific plural (-pādaiḥ); this favours a verse, not a person. The Tibetan translation, spyod pa pa glu dbyangs zhabs kyis gsungs, uses the honorific zhabs and so treats it as a person, roughly ‘the song-master of conduct’. Its shes pa'i tshig las is probably a slip for zhes pa'i tshig las (iti vacanāt).

For yogināṃ paramārthavidām, ‘for yogis who know the ultimate’, the Tibetan has rnal 'byor pas don dam par rig pas so, ‘because the yogi knows in the ultimate sense’. The printed etadartha is read etadarthaṃ.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena svakīyānuśaṃsām āhuḥ—
je je ityādi | ye ye bhāv[āḥ] utpannās te te bhāvā vilayaṃ gatāḥ | eṣām utpādabhaṅgeṣu saṃvṛtisatyasvabhāvaparijñānena guruprasādatvāt kṛṣṇācāryacaraṇā viśiṣṭamanasaḥ pariśuddhabhūtāḥ |
tathā cāgamaḥ—
bhavasyaiva parijñāne nirvāṇam iti kathyate |
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks in [praise]{anusamsa} of himself: ‘Each one that…’ and so on. Whatever things arose, those things have gone to dissolution. Through fully knowing, in their [arising and perishing]{utpada-bhanga}, the nature of [conventional]{samvrti} truth, by the grace of the [guru]{guru}, the venerable [Kṛṣṇācārya]{p-kanha} became of distinguished mind, purified. So the scripture says: ‘When [existence]{bhava} itself is fully known, that is called [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}.’
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.07.m5) calls this couplet Kāṇha’s praise of himself: whatever things arose have dissolved, and knowing by the guru’s grace the nature of conventional truth in their arising and perishing, Kṛṣṇācārya became ‘of distinguished mind’, purified. His paraphrase thus puts arising and perishing for ‘[coming and going]{coming-and-going}’, and a distinguished mind for ‘[downcast]{vimana}’.

citations.quoted: When existence itself is fully known, that is called nirvāṇa.

flags.note: In the quotation the Tibetan translation has srid pa'i de nyid yongs shes na, ‘if the reality (or the very nature) of existence is fully known’, for bhavasyaiva, ‘of existence itself’; de nyid probably renders eva. In the paraphrase it makes Kṛṣṇācārya's mind (yid) the subject of ‘became purified’.

His Sanskrit rendering of 4a supplies bhāvāḥ, ‘things’, as the subject of ‘came’ and ‘went’, which become utpanna, ‘arisen’, and vilayaṃ gata, ‘dissolved’. utpādabhaṅgeṣu, ‘in arising and perishing’, stands where 4b has abaṇāgabaṇe, ‘in coming and going’, and viśiṣṭamanasaḥ where it has bimana. These are paraphrases, not explicit glosses, so I list no equations.
anuśaṃsā, here ‘praise’ (Tibetan rjes su bsngags pa), can also mean ‘benefit, blessing’ in Buddhist Sanskrit. I propose an entry because the word recurs (cp.07.m6, and the comment on song 4).

segments.translit:
caturthapadena cātmānuśaṃsām āhuḥ |
heri se ityādi | svayam ātmānaṃ saṃbodhya vadanti, bho kṛṣṇavajrapādāḥ pañcakramānupūrvyā punar jinapuraṃ mahāsukhapuraṃ atīva mama sannihitaṃ vartate |
tathā ca nāgārjunapādāḥ |
utpattikramasaṃsthānāṃ utpannakramakāṅkṣiṇāṃ |
upāyaś caiṣa saṃbuddhau sopānam iva nirmitaḥ ||
segments.translation: And with the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks in [praise]{anusamsa} of himself: ‘Look…’ and so on. Addressing himself, he says: ‘O [Kṛṣṇavajrapāda]{p-kanha}, through the [five stages]{pancakrama} in their order, the [city of the Jina]{jinapura}, the city of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, is again very near to me.’ So [Nāgārjuna]{p-nagarjuna} says: ‘For those established in the [generation stage]{utpattikrama} who long for the [completion stage]{nispannakrama}, this means has been built, like a stairway, toward full [awakening]{bodhi}.’
segments.note: Munidatta (cp.07.m6) calls this couplet Kāṇha’s self-praise (the Tibetan translation: praise of the path). Addressing himself, Kāṇha says that through the [five stages]{pancakrama} in order the [city of the Jina]{jinapura}, the city of great bliss, is very near him. Nāgārjuna’s verse calls this means a stairway for those in the generation stage who long for the completion stage.

equations.en: the city of great bliss (mahāsukhapura), in apposition

citations.quoted: For those established in the generation stage who long for the completion stage, this means has been built, like a stairway, toward full awakening.
citations.work: Nāgārjuna (named by Munidatta), Pañcakrama; the work is my identification from memory, unverified

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) introduces the couplet as lam gyi rjes su bsngags pa, ‘praise of the path’, where the Sanskrit has ātmānuśaṃsā, ‘praise of himself’ (compare svakīyānuśaṃsā in cp.07.m5, which it renders rang gi rjes su bsngags pa).

For jinapuraṃ … mama sannihitaṃ, ‘the city of the Jina … near to me’, the Tibetan has rgyal po'i pho brang … grong khyer pa dag la shin du nye bar 'gyur, ‘the king's palace … becomes very near to the city(-dwellers?)’. rgyal po'i, ‘king's’, as in its version of line 5a, may be a slip for rgyal ba'i, ‘the Jina's’; grong khyer pa dag la is unclear and nothing renders mama, ‘to me’. It also makes the five stages a condition: rim pa lnga sngon du song na, ‘once the five stages have gone before’.

The printed saṃbuddhau, ‘for full awakening’, is translated as it stands. The Tibetan rdzogs sangs rgyas kyis, ‘by the perfect buddhas’, reflects saṃbuddhaiḥ, which I believe is the verse's usual reading: ‘this means was built by the perfect buddhas like a stairway’. The printed ceṣa is read caiṣa.

utpannakrama- stands where the verse is usually cited with niṣpannakrama-, ‘completion stage’; the Tibetan rdzogs pa'i rim pa confirms that sense, so I translate ‘completion stage’. punar, ‘again’ (Tibetan slar yang), may simply mean ‘then, moreover’.

proposals.definition: Praise or commendation (Sanskrit anuśaṃsā; in Buddhist Sanskrit also ‘benefit, blessing’). Munidatta uses it to introduce couplets in which the poet speaks of what he has attained: ‘his own praise’ (cp.07.m5), ‘praise of himself’ (cp.07.m6). The Tibetan translation has rjes su bsngags pa, ‘praise’.
proposals.rationale: A recurring formula of Munidatta’s for the poet’s self-praise (cp.07.m5, cp.07.m6; also yoginyā anuśaṃsām āha in the comment on song 4). A reader meeting ‘praise of himself’ may want the word and its other sense, ‘benefit’, explained once.

questions: Name forms: Munidatta calls the poet Kṛṣṇācāryapāda, Kṛṣṇācāryacaraṇa and, addressing himself, Kṛṣṇavajrapāda (cp.07.m3, cp.07.m6). I used the listed variant ‘Kṛṣṇācārya’ for the first two, dropping the honorifics, but kept ‘Kṛṣṇavajrapāda’ in the self-address, although it is not a listed variant of p-kanha. Add it as a variant, or normalize to Kṛṣṇācārya or Kāṇha? Likewise I wrote ‘Sarahapāda’ (a listed variant) but plain ‘Nāgārjuna’, since ‘Nāgārjunapāda’ is not listed.

Downcast or distinguished? In both the Sanskrit and the Tibetan, Munidatta’s paraphrases of 1b and 4b (cp.07.m2, cp.07.m5) have viśiṣṭamanas, ‘of distinguished mind’, where the song has bimana. The Tibetan translation of the song itself (rnam mi dga’, yid mi bde) supports the draft’s ‘downcast’. Should the line notes on 1b and 4b, which are outside this task, set out the divergence?

cp.07.m4: the quoted Apabhraṃśa verse is garbled, and I took the numbers (thirty-seven, nine, thirty-eight) from the Tibetan. Keep them, or mark the numbers as uncertain in the translation itself? Also, do you accept ‘a verse of a song of conduct’ for caryāpādena, rather than the Tibetan’s reading of it as an author’s name?
cp.07.m3: I translated sa tanmayatvāt literally (‘since it is made of that’). The Tibetan’s thams cad suggests sarva-, ‘since everything is made of it’. Adopt the Tibetan-supported reading?
Munidatta’s comment on the last couplet (cp.07.m6) explains only 5a; he passes over 5b (‘it does not enter my heart’). Should the reader be told?
Proposal anusamsa (‘praise’): is it worth an entry, or should the word stay unmarked?
